madhura avastha paka.title: Madhura Avastha Pāka
madhura avastha paka.body: Madhura Avastha Pāka is the Sanskrit term for the sweet stage of digestion. It represents the principle of Kapha-predominant liquefaction and is associated with the nourishment of immature, asthāyi, Rasa Dhātu in the body. Located on the tip of the tongue, jihvā, and energetically linked to the thyroid, Madhura stimulates the emotions of joy and contentment. Its Vipāka, the post-digestive effect, is Madhura, which is anabolic and increases Kapha Dosha.

bodhaka kapha.title: Bodhaka Kapha
bodhaka kapha.body: Bodhaka Kapha is the subdosha of Kapha related to the water element. It is primarily located in the mouth and oral cavity and is responsible for salivary secretions, taste, swallowing, and speech.

oral cavity.title: Oral cavity
oral cavity.body: The oral cavity, or mouth, is the first part of the digestive tract, extending from the lips to the back of the throat, connecting to the pharynx. It contains essential structures like the teeth, tongue, palate, and openings for salivary glands. Its key functions include mechanically breaking down food through chewing and starting chemical digestion with saliva, shaping airflow and producing sounds for speech, evaluating food through sensory receptors called taste buds, and serving as a secondary airway when nasal breathing is restricted.

the bhutas.title: The bhūtas
the bhutas.body: The five great elements: earth, water, fire, air, and ether.

madhura.title: Madhura
madhura.body: Madhura is the Sanskrit term for the sweet taste, the first of the six essential rasas. It represents the principle of anabolic growth and is associated with the earth and water elements in the body.

prthivi.title: Prthivī
prthivi.body: Prthivī is the Sanskrit term for the Earth element, the fifth of the five basic elements (pañcha mahābhūtas). It represents the principle of stability and is associated with mechanical energy in the body.

apas.title: Āpas
apas.body: Āpas is the Sanskrit term for the Water element, the fourth of the five basic elements, pañcha mahābhūtas. It represents the principle of cohesiveness and is associated with chemical energy in the body.

saliva.title: Saliva
saliva.body: Saliva is a clear secretion of the salivary glands that is mixed with food during the mechanical process of mastication. Its primary functions include acting as a lubricant to help food pass through the gastrointestinal tract and initiating chemical digestion by using the enzyme amylase to break down starches. By mixing with chewed food to form a bolus, saliva facilitates swallowing and allows chemicals to dissolve so they can stimulate taste receptors on the tongue. Additionally, saliva serves as a vital component of the body's nonspecific immune defenses by cleaning microbes from the teeth and gums and using the antimicrobial enzyme lysozyme to destroy pathogenic bacteria.

salivary glands.title: Salivary glands
salivary glands.body: Glands that secrete saliva into the mouth.

parotid.title: Parotid
parotid.body: The parotid gland is the largest of the three main salivary glands, located just below and in front of each ear. Its primary function is to secrete a thin, watery saliva rich in the enzyme amylase, which initiates the digestion of starches. This saliva lubricates the mouth, making it easier to chew and swallow food, while also helping to wash away bacteria and protect tooth enamel from cavities.

submandibular.title: Submandibular
submandibular.body: The submandibular gland consists of a pair of major salivary glands located beneath the lower jaw. Its primary function is to produce up to 70% of resting saliva, which lubricates the mouth, facilitates swallowing, chemically breaks down starches through enzymes, and protects against oral bacteria and decay.

sublingual.title: Sublingual
sublingual.body: The sublingual gland is the smallest of the major salivary glands, located under the mucous membrane in the floor of the mouth, on either side of the tongue. Its primary function is to secrete thick, mucus-rich saliva, which lubricates food for easier swallowing, keeps the mouth moist, and aids in early digestion. The mucus coats food to form a slippery bolus for swallowing and protects the oral mucosa from dryness and irritation.

mastication.title: Mastication
mastication.body: Mastication is the mechanical process of chewing where food is physically smashed or broken into smaller pieces by the teeth while being positioned by the tongue and the muscles of the cheeks and lips. Its primary function is to prepare food for swallowing and further processing by mixing it with saliva, which lubricates the mass into a bolus and initiates the chemical breakdown of starches through the enzyme amylase. This essential stage of mechanical digestion is driven by the coordinated action of several muscles of the head and face, most notably the temporalis, masseter, and the medial and lateral pterygoids.

mechanical digestion.title: Mechanical digestion
mechanical digestion.body: Mechanical digestion is the metabolic process that physically smashes, grinds, or breaks down food substances into smaller, more usable particles. This process begins in the oral cavity through mastication, where the teeth and tongue work together to smash food and mix it with saliva to form a bolus. Mechanical digestion continues in the stomach as strong smooth muscle contractions churn and mix food with gastric juices to create a semiliquid substance known as chyme. Within the small intestine, this process involves segmentation, which uses alternating smooth muscle contractions to mix and churn the chyme. The primary function of these mechanical actions is to physically break apart food particles and mix them with digestive secretions, which prepares the substance for chemical digestion and nutrient absorption.

chemical digestion.title: Chemical digestion
chemical digestion.body: Chemical digestion is the metabolic process that utilizes specialized enzymes and acids to decompose food substances into smaller, usable molecules. This complex series of reactions begins in the mouth as salivary amylase starts breaking down starches and continues in the stomach, where hydrochloric acid and pepsin initiate the breakdown of proteins. The majority of chemical digestion takes place in the small intestine, where secretions like pancreatic juice—containing lipase, trypsin, and amylase—work alongside intestinal enzymes to dissolve carbohydrates, fats, and proteins into their simplest forms. The primary function of this process is to transform food into basic nutrients that can be absorbed into the blood or lymph for transportation to cells, providing the necessary materials for energy, tissue repair, and renewal.

amylase.title: Amylase
amylase.body: Amylase is a specialized enzyme primarily responsible for the chemical digestion of starches, which are a type of carbohydrate. Secreted by the salivary glands, it begins the process of chemical digestion in the mouth during mastication, breaking down complex starches into smaller, simpler molecules that can sometimes be noticed as a slightly sweet taste if starchy foods like bread are held in the mouth for a few minutes. Amylase is also a primary component of the alkaline pancreatic juice produced by the pancreas. This version of the enzyme is transported to the small intestine, where it continues the work of breaking down carbohydrates that were not fully digested in the mouth.

bolus.title: Bolus
bolus.body: A bolus is a soft, lubricated mass formed in the oral cavity when food is thoroughly chewed and mixed with saliva. Its primary function is to be swallowed via the involuntary reflex of deglutition, which moves the mixture through the pharynx and into the esophagus. Once in the esophagus, mucus secretions further lubricate the bolus as peristalsis—a series of wave-like smooth muscle contractions—propels it toward the stomach for the next stage of digestion.

jihva.title: Jihvā
jihva.body: Jihva is the Sanskrit term for the tongue.

tongue.title: Tongue
tongue.body: The muscular organ of taste and speech.

hypothalamus.title: Hypothalamus
hypothalamus.body: A brain region governing many automatic body functions.

sadhaka pitta.title: Sādhaka Pitta
sadhaka pitta.body: Sādhaka Pitta is the subdosha of Pitta related to the ether element. It is primarily located in the brain's grey matter and represents the principles of conscious thinking, emotions, and comprehension.

prana vayu.title: Prāna Vāyu
prana vayu.body: Prāna Vāyu is the subdosha of Vāta related to the ether element. It is primarily located in the head, brain, and synaptic cleft, represents the principle of inhalation, and moves in a downward and inward direction.

pharynx.title: Pharynx
pharynx.body: The pharynx, commonly referred to as the throat, is a muscular tube situated behind the mouth and nasal cavity. It serves as a critical passageway for both the respiratory and digestive systems, directing inhaled air to the larynx and facilitating the transport of food into the esophagus. The pharynx fulfills three primary functions: it channels air from the nasal and oral cavities to the larynx and lungs; its muscular walls propel food and liquids into the esophagus, preventing aspiration into the trachea; and it contributes to phonation while housing the tonsils, which are instrumental in immune defense against infections.

esophagus.title: Esophagus
esophagus.body: The esophagus is a muscular tube that connects the pharynx to the stomach. It serves a critical role in the transport of swallowed food and liquids through a process known as peristalsis, which involves a series of coordinated wave-like muscle contractions. This mechanism allows for the effective movement of food into the stomach, even when in horizontal positions. The esophagus is equipped with sphincter muscles at both the upper and lower ends, functioning as gatekeepers. The lower esophageal sphincter is particularly important, as it prevents the reflux of gastric acid into the esophagus, thereby protecting it from potential damage.

peristalsis.title: Peristalsis
peristalsis.body: Peristalsis is a series of involuntary, wave-like smooth muscle contractions that function to propel contents forward through the body's various muscular tubes. Within the digestive system, these coordinated contractions move a bolus through the esophagus and push chyme through the stomach and small intestine to facilitate nutrient processing and absorption. Beyond digestion, peristalsis is essential for transporting urine through the ureters to the bladder and moving an ovum through the fallopian tubes toward the uterus.

fundus.title: Fundus
fundus.body: The upper, dome-shaped part of the stomach.

samana vayu.title: Samāna Vāyu
samana vayu.body: Sāmana Vāyu is the subdosha of Vāta related to the fire element. It is primarily located in the small intestine and navel, represents the principle of digestion, and moves in a linear direction.

rasa dhatu.title: Rasa Dhātu
rasa dhatu.body:
Rasa Dhātu is the Sanskrit term for the plasma or lymph tissue, the first of the biological tissues. It represents the principle of nutrition and immunity, prīnana, serving as the essential "juice of life" that circulates through the cardiovascular and lymphatic systems to provide sustenance to every cell in the body.

Upa-Dhātu: the top layer of the skin, tvak, lactation stanya, and menstruation, rajah

Mala: Poshaka Kapha, precursor Kapha, which manifests as mucus, kleda

thyroid.title: Thyroid
thyroid.body: The gland in the neck that regulates metabolism.

lungs.title: Lungs
lungs.body: The organs of breathing and gas exchange.

vipaka.title: Vipāka
vipaka.body: Vipāka is the Sanskrit term for the post-digestive effect, the third of the three pharmacological principles. It represents the principle of metabolic transformation and is associated with the elemental combinations of the three resulting post-digestive tastes: pruthivī, earth and āpas, water (madhura, sweet and anabolic), pruthivī, earth and āgni, fire (amla, sour and metabolic), and āgni, fire and vāyu, air (katu, pungent and catabolic) in the body.

anabolic.title: Anabolic
anabolic.body: Anabolic/ Anabolism is a metabolic building-up process where complex molecules are constructed from simpler ones to create or repair tissue or to store nutrients for future use. This process is essential for tissue growth and repair through activities like protein synthesis, where amino acids are linked together to build cells and tissues. Beyond structural repair, anabolism is responsible for the synthesis of vital molecules such as hormones, neurotransmitters, and ligands. It also serves a critical role in nutrient storage, exemplified by the conversion of excess glucose into glycogen, which is then stored in the liver and skeletal muscles for later energy needs

kapha dosha.title: Kapha Dosha
kapha dosha.body: Kapha Dosha is the Sanskrit term for the water or structure principle, the third of the three biological organizations, tridosha. It represents the principle of substance, providing the body's structure, lubrication, and cohesiveness, and is associated with the water and earth elements.

amashaya.title: Āmāshaya
amashaya.body: Āmāshaya is the Sanskrit term for the stomach. It is the main site of Kapha and Pitta Dosha and the therapeutic site for Kapha Dosha.

bhutas.title: Bhūtas
bhutas.body: The five great elements: earth, water, fire, air, and ether.

amla.title: Amla
amla.body: Amla is the Sanskrit term for the sour taste, the second of the six essential rasas. It represents the principle of metabolic stimulation and is associated with the earth and fire elements in the body.

agni.title: Āgni
agni.body: Āgni is the Sanskrit term for the Fire element, the third of the five basic elements, pañcha mahābhūtas. It represents the principle of transformation and is associated with radiant energy in the body.

jathara agni.title: Jāthara Āgni
jathara agni.body: Jāthara Āgni is the Sanskrit term for the central digestive fire, the main Āgni out of the 40 types of Āgni.

pachaka pitta.title: Pāchaka Pitta
pachaka pitta.body: Pāchaka Pitta is the subdosha of Pitta related to the fire element. It is primarily located in the small intestine and stomach and represents the principles of digestion, absorption, and assimilation of food.

hydrochloric acid hcl.title: Hydrochloric acid (HCl)
hydrochloric acid hcl.body: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is a highly acidic electrolyte compound secreted by the stomach as a primary component of gastric juice. Its primary digestive functions include initiating the chemical breakdown of proteins and activating the enzyme pepsin from its inactive form, pepsinogen. Beyond digestion, it serves as a critical nonspecific immune defense by killing or destroying bacteria and other pathogens that enter the body with food. Because of its potency, the stomach produces a protective layer of mucus to prevent the acid from damaging the stomach wall or causing ulcers.

pathogens.title: Pathogens
pathogens.body: Pathogens are microscopic substances or agents, including viruses, bacteria, fungi, parasites, chemicals, and particles, that cause disease and challenge the body’s health and well-being. Their primary function is to create physiologic disruptions that lead to infectious diseases, often by invading body cells to replicate or by triggering harmful immune responses. Most pathogens possess unique chemical markers called antigens, which allow the immune system to identify them as foreign and initiate specific defensive actions. To protect the organism, these invaders are trapped by mucous membranes in internal passageways, blocked from the brain by the blood-brain barrier, or filtered from circulation by the spleen and lymph nodes to be destroyed by phagocytes.

pepsin.title: Pepsin
pepsin.body: Pepsin is a potent protein-digesting enzyme produced by the stomach that plays a critical role in the chemical digestion of food. To protect the stomach wall, it is first secreted in an inactive form called pepsinogen, which is subsequently activated into functional pepsin by the presence of hydrochloric acid. Its primary function is to initiate the breakdown of proteins into smaller, absorbable components as food is processed into a semiliquid mass known as chyme.

hcl.title: HCl
hcl.body: HCI (hydrochloric acid) is a highly acidic electrolyte compound secreted by the stomach as a primary component of gastric juice. Its primary digestive functions include initiating the chemical breakdown of proteins and activating the enzyme pepsin from its inactive form, pepsinogen. Beyond digestion, it serves as a critical nonspecific immune defense by killing or destroying bacteria and other pathogens that enter the body with food. Because of its potency, the stomach produces a protective layer of mucus to prevent the acid from damaging the stomach wall or causing ulcers.

kledaka kapha.title: Kledaka Kapha
kledaka kapha.body: Kledaka Kapha is the subdosha of Kapha related to the fire element. It is primarily located in the stomach and represents the principles of gastric secretion, digestion, absorption, and the nourishment of rasa, plasma.

mucous membrane.title: Mucous membrane
mucous membrane.body: Mucous membranes are epithelial membranes consisting of a simple epithelial layer attached to a thin basement membrane that line cavities open to the external environment, such as the respiratory, digestive, and urinary tracts. Their primary function is to protect the body by secreting a thick substance called mucus, which acts as a physical barrier to trap invading pathogens and foreign particles. In the respiratory system, they also serve to warm and humidify air while using cilia to move trapped microbes out of the body. Furthermore, these membranes safeguard internal linings from wear and erosion, such as protecting the stomach wall from the corrosive effects of hydrochloric acid.

shleshma dhara kala.title: Shleshma Dhārā Kalā
shleshma dhara kala.body: Shleshma Dhārā Kalā is the Sanskrit term for the gastric mucous membrane, one of the internal membranous structures, Kalās, located in the stomach, āmāshaya. It represents the principle of gastric protection and lubrication, producing mucosal secretions that shield the stomach wall from the corrosive intensity of digestive acids and enzymes, and is associated with the water and earth elements in the body.

chyme.title: Chyme
chyme.body: Chyme is a semiliquid mixture of food and digestive juices, including hydrochloric acid and pepsin, that is formed in the stomach as strong smooth muscle contractions churn and mix its contents. Its primary function is to transport partially digested food into the small intestine for the next stages of chemical digestion and nutrient absorption. This process is regulated by the pyloric sphincter, which opens to allow only a small amount of the highly acidic chyme into the duodenum at one time. Once it enters the small intestine, chyme is neutralized by alkaline secretions like bicarbonates and further processed through segmentation, which continues to mix and churn the mixture to facilitate the breakdown of nutrients by various enzymes.

pyloric valve.title: Pyloric valve
pyloric valve.body: The opening from the stomach into the small intestine.

pyloric sphincter.title: Pyloric sphincter
pyloric sphincter.body: The pyloric sphincter is a thick ring of smooth muscle located at the distal end of the stomach, where it connects to the duodenum of the small intestine. This involuntary valve regulates the flow of partially digested food, known as chyme, from the stomach into the intestines. It opens intermittently to release small, manageable amounts of chyme, facilitating proper digestion and nutrient absorption. Additionally, it closes to prevent the backflow of intestinal contents into the stomach and to protect the small intestine from exposure to harsh gastric acid.

duodenum.title: Duodenum
duodenum.body: The duodenum is the first and shortest section of the small intestine, connecting the stomach to the jejunum. It is C-shaped and about 10 inches long. Its main function is chemical digestion; it receives partially digested food (chyme) from the stomach and mixes it with bile from the liver and digestive enzymes from the pancreas to break down proteins, fats, and carbohydrates.

virya.title: Vīrya
virya.body: Vīrya is the Sanskrit term for potent energy, the second of the three pharmacological principles. It represents the principle of thermal potency and is associated with the āgni, fire element (for heating energy, ushna) and the āpas, water element (for cooling energy, shīta) in the body.

ushna.title: Ushna Guna
ushna.body: Ushna is the Sanskrit term for the hot quality, representing the principle of digestion and is associated with increased circulation in the body.

shita.title: Shīta Guna
shita.body: Shīta is the Sanskrit term for the cold quality, representing the principle of contraction and is associated with reduced metabolic rate in the body.

metabolic.title: Metabolic
metabolic.body: Metabolic/ Metabolism encompasses the sum of all biochemical reactions and chemical processes that occur within a cell or the human organism to sustain life. Its primary function is to transform nutrients into usable forms to provide energy for cellular work and the necessary materials for tissue growth, repair, and reproduction. These processes are divided into two essential categories: anabolism, which constructs complex molecules from simpler ones to build or repair tissue and store nutrients for future use, and catabolism, which chemically breaks down complex molecules into smaller particles to release or create energy in the form of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Furthermore, these metabolic activities serve a critical role in regulating body temperature by generating most of the body's internal heat as a byproduct of energy production.

pitta dosha.title: Pitta Dosha
pitta dosha.body: Pitta Dosha is the Sanskrit term for the fire or transformation principle, the second of the three biological organizations, tridosha. It represents the principle of transformation, governing digestion, metabolism, and body temperature, and is associated with the fire and water elements.

lavana avastha paka.title: Lavana Avastha Pāka
lavana avastha paka.body: Lavana Avastha Pāka is the Sanskrit term for the salty stage of digestion. It represents the principle of Pitta-predominant emulsification and is associated with the nourishment of immature, asthāyi, Māmsa and Meda Dhātus in the body. Located on the posterior outer sides of the tongue, jihvā, and energetically linked to the kidneys, Lavana stimulates emotions of attachment, greed, and possessiveness. Its Vipāka, the post-digestive effect, is Madhura, which is anabolic and increases Kapha Dosha.

lavana.title: Lavana
lavana.body: Lavana is the Sanskrit term for the salty taste, the third of the six essential rasas. It represents the principle of buffering and lubrication and is associated with the water and fire elements in the body.

stomach.title: Stomach
stomach.body: The stomach is a muscular organ in the upper abdomen that serves as a temporary reservoir and processing center for ingested food. It performs mechanical digestion through churning and chemical digestion using hydrochloric acid and enzymes to create a semi-liquid mixture called chyme, which is gradually passed into the small intestine. The stomach muscles contract and relax to churn food into a smooth liquid, while hydrochloric acid and enzymes break down proteins and kill harmful bacteria.

the small intestine secretes.title: The small intestine secretes
the small intestine secretes.body: The small intestine releases its own digestive enzymes.

mucus.title: Mucus
mucus.body: Mucous is a term primarily associated with mucous membranes (or mucosa), which are epithelial layers that line body cavities open to the external environment, such as the respiratory, digestive, and urinary tracts. These membranes secrete a thick, clear substance known as mucus that serves as a vital protective barrier and lubricant for internal passageways. In the digestive system, it facilitates the movement of food while shielding the tract's walls from wear, erosion, and corrosive acids. Within the respiratory tract, mucus further functions to warm and humidify inhaled air and trap foreign particles or pathogens so they can be safely removed from the body.

small intestine.title: Small intestine
small intestine.body: Where most digestion and absorption of nutrients occurs.

liver.title: Liver
liver.body: The liver is the body's largest internal organ, weighing about 1.5 kg and located in the upper right abdomen. It serves as a vital processing center, performing over 500 essential functions. Key roles include digestion and energy management through bile production for fat breakdown, nutrient processing, and blood sugar regulation by storing excess glucose as glycogen. Additionally, the liver detoxifies harmful substances, drugs, and alcohol, converting waste products like ammonia into safe urea for excretion. It also synthesizes essential blood proteins, such as albumin and clotting factors, while storing important vitamins and minerals like iron.

pancreas.title: Pancreas
pancreas.body: The pancreas is a vital gland located behind the stomach, essential for both digestion and metabolism. It has two primary functions: the exocrine function produces powerful enzymes such as amylase, lipase, and protease, which are released into the small intestine to break down carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. The endocrine function involves releasing hormones directly into the bloodstream, particularly insulin to lower blood sugar levels and glucagon to raise them, thereby maintaining energy balance in the body.

duct.title: Duct
duct.body: A tube carrying secretions, such as bile or enzymes.

secretin.title: Secretin
secretin.body: Secretin is a local hormone produced and secreted by the duodenum of the small intestine that plays a vital role in coordinating the digestive process. Its primary function is to stimulate the pancreas to release bicarbonates and water into the gastrointestinal tract. This alkaline secretion is essential for neutralizing the hydrochloric acid found in highly acidic chyme, which raises the pH level and effectively inactivates the enzyme pepsin to prepare the mixture for further digestion and absorption within the small intestine.

bicarbonates.title: Bicarbonates
bicarbonates.body: Bicarbonates (HCO3) are inorganic salts that serve as vital electrolytes, playing a central role in maintaining the body's homeostatic pH balance. In the respiratory system, approximately 80% of the carbon dioxide produced by tissues is converted into bicarbonate ions for transport through the bloodstream to the lungs for elimination. Within the digestive system, the pancreas secretes bicarbonates into the small intestine to neutralize highly acidic chyme. This process protects the intestinal lining and creates the necessary alkaline environment for digestive enzymes to function. Furthermore, the kidneys assist in regulating these electrolyte levels by either reabsorbing or eliminating bicarbonate ions to ensure the blood remains within its essential, slightly alkaline range.

kloma agni.title: Kloma Āgni
kloma agni.body: Kloma Āgni is the Sanskrit term for the pancreatic fire, one of the 40 types of Āgni located in the pancreas and choroid plexuses.

hydrochloric acid.title: Hydrochloric acid
hydrochloric acid.body: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is a highly acidic electrolyte compound secreted by the stomach as a primary component of gastric juice. Its primary digestive functions include initiating the chemical breakdown of proteins and activating the enzyme pepsin from its inactive form, pepsinogen. Beyond digestion, it serves as a critical nonspecific immune defense by killing or destroying bacteria and other pathogens that enter the body with food. Because of its potency, the stomach produces a protective layer of mucus to prevent the acid from damaging the stomach wall or causing ulcers.

cholecystokinin.title: Cholecystokinin
cholecystokinin.body: Cholecystokinin (CCK) is a local hormone produced and secreted by the small intestine, specifically the duodenum, that plays a vital role in coordinating chemical digestion. Its primary functions include stimulating the pancreas to release digestive enzymes and signaling the gallbladder and liver to discharge bile into the gastrointestinal tract. Furthermore, CCK serves as a key integrator between body systems; because receptors for the hormone are also located in the brain and spleen, it effectively links digestive activity to both the nervous and immune systems.

cck.title: CCK
cck.body: Cholecystokinin (CCK) is a local hormone produced and secreted by the small intestine, specifically the duodenum, that plays a vital role in coordinating chemical digestion. Its primary functions include stimulating the pancreas to release digestive enzymes and signaling the gallbladder and liver to discharge bile into the gastrointestinal tract. Furthermore, CCK serves as a key integrator between body systems; because receptors for the hormone are also located in the brain and spleen, it effectively links digestive activity to both the nervous and immune systems.

pancreatic digestive enzymes.title: Pancreatic digestive enzymes
pancreatic digestive enzymes.body: Pancreatic digestive enzymes are biological catalysts produced by the exocrine cells of the pancreas and delivered to the duodenum through the pancreatic duct. These enzymes, which include amylase, lipase, and trypsin, are essential components of alkaline pancreatic juice. Their primary function is to coordinate the chemical digestion of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins by breaking them down into simpler, absorbable molecules. By neutralizing acidic chyme from the stomach and performing the majority of nutrient decomposition in the small intestine, they provide the body with the basic nutrients required for energy production and tissue repair.

bile.title: Bile
bile.body: Bile is a yellow-brown or greenish fluid produced by hepatocytes in the liver and then concentrated and stored in the gallbladder until it is required for digestion. Its primary function is to act as a fat emulsifier, physically breaking apart large fat globules into smaller particles so that digestive enzymes can more effectively process lipids within the small intestine. This emulsification is critical for facilitating the proper absorption of fats. Additionally, bile serves as a vehicle for the liver to eliminate bilirubin, a yellow-orange pigment produced during the breakdown of old red blood cells.

ranjaka pitta.title: Rañjaka Pitta
ranjaka pitta.body: Rānjaka Pitta is the subdosha of Pitta related to the water element. It is primarily located in the liver, spleen, and stomach (as an intrinsic factor), is involved in the production of bile and liver enzymes, and gives blood its color.

gallbladder.title: Gallbladder
gallbladder.body: The gallbladder is a small, pear-shaped organ located underneath the liver. Its main job is to store and concentrate bile, a fluid made by the liver. When you eat, the gallbladder contracts and releases bile into the small intestine. This bile helps break down and digest fats, making it easier for your body to absorb.

kidneys.title: Kidneys
kidneys.body: Organs that filter the blood and form urine.

katu avastha paka.title: Katu Avastha Pāka
katu avastha paka.body: Katu Avastha Pāka is the Sanskrit term for the pungent stage of digestion. It represents the principle of Vāta-predominant thermogenesis and is associated with the nourishment of immature, asthāyi, Asthi Dhātu in the body. Located on the central part of the tongue, jihvā, anterior to the bitter area, Katu is energetically linked to the heart, stomach, and diaphragm and stimulates emotions of anger, irritation, and frustration. Its Vipāka, the post-digestive effect, is Katu, which is catabolic and increases Vāta Dosha.

jejunum.title: Jejunum
jejunum.body: The jejunum is the middle section of the small intestine, situated between the duodenum and the ileum. It plays a crucial role in the rapid absorption of digested nutrients, including carbohydrates, proteins, and fats, as well as water into the bloodstream.

katu.title: Katu
katu.body: Katu is the Sanskrit term for the pungent taste, the fourth of the six essential rasas. It represents the principle of circulation and cleansing and is associated with the fire and air elements in the body.

vayu.title: Vāyu
vayu.body: Vāyu is the Sanskrit term for the Air element, the second of the five basic elements, pañcha mahābhūtas. It represents the principle of movement and is associated with electrical energy in the body.

thermogenesis.title: Thermogenesis
thermogenesis.body: Thermogenesis is the process of heat production in the body. This process occurs as a primary byproduct of metabolism, specifically catabolism, where the chemical breakdown of nutrients to create energy (ATP) releases internal heat. Additionally, muscle contractions generate significant heat when ATP is broken down to power movement. The primary function of this heat generation is to regulate body temperature and maintain homeostasis.

gi tract.title: GI tract
gi tract.body: The gastrointestinal tract — the whole digestive passage.

ileum.title: Ileum
ileum.body: The ileum is the final and longest section of the small intestine, connecting the jejunum to the large intestine. Its main functions include absorbing essential nutrients such as Vitamin B12 and bile salts, completing digestion, and protecting the gut from harmful bacteria through specialized immune tissues called Peyer's patches.

colon.title: Colon
colon.body: The main part of the large intestine.

ahara rasa.title: Āhāra Rasa
ahara rasa.body: Āhāra Rasa is the nutritive juice or chyle that serves as the post-digestive precursor for the nourishment of all seven bodily tissues, Dhātus, and every cell in the body.

chyle.title: Chyle
chyle.body: Chyle is a cloudy white or pale-yellow liquid product of digestion that is primarily composed of emulsified fats. Its function is to transport these long-chain fatty acids after they are absorbed by specialized lymphatic capillaries, known as lacteals, located in the small intestine. During the digestive process, chyle is collected by the lymphatic system and transported through the thoracic duct into the subclavian veins, where it enters the bloodstream and is eventually delivered to the liver for processing.

heart.title: Heart
heart.body: The organ that pumps blood through the body.

diaphragm.title: Diaphragm
diaphragm.body: The muscle beneath the lungs that drives breathing.

vata dosha.title: Vāta Dosha
vata dosha.body: Vāta Dosha is the Sanskrit term for the air or movement principle, the first of the three biological organizations, tridosha. It represents the principle of mobility, which regulates all bodily activity, and is associated with the ether and air elements.

tikta avastha paka.title: Tikta Avastha Pāka
tikta avastha paka.body: Tikta Avastha Pāka is the Sanskrit term for the bitter stage of digestion. It represents the principle of Vāta-predominant absorption and is associated with the nourishment of immature, asthāyi, Majjā Dhātu in the body. Located on the central part of the tongue, jihvā posterior to the pungent area, Tikta is energetically linked to the liver, spleen, and pancreas and stimulates emotions of loneliness, isolation, and separation. Its Vipāka, the post-digestive effect, is Katu, which is catabolic and increases Vāta Dosha.

tikta.title: Tikta
tikta.body: Tikta is the Sanskrit term for the bitter taste, the fifth of the six essential rasas. It represents the principle of detoxification and scraping and is associated with the air and ether elements in the body.

akasha.title: Ākāsha
akasha.body: Ākāsha is the Sanskrit term for the Ether or Space element, the first of the five basic elements, pañcha mahābhūtas. It represents the principle of freedom and is associated with nuclear energy in the body.

villi.title: Villi
villi.body: Tiny finger-like projections in the intestine that absorb nutrients.

spleen.title: Spleen
spleen.body: An organ involved in blood filtering and immunity.

catabolic.title: Catabolic
catabolic.body: Catabolic/ Catabolism refers to the metabolic category of processes that chemically break down or decompose complex molecules and nutrients into smaller, more usable particles. Its primary function is to provide the body with accessible nutrients and to release or create energy—specifically adenosine triphosphate (ATP)—required for all cellular work and muscle contraction. Key examples of catabolic processes include glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, where glucose is broken down to produce ATP, and the subsequent breakdown of ATP itself to release its stored energy. Furthermore, these catabolic activities are responsible for generating most of the body's internal heat.

kashaya avastha paka.title: Kashāya Avastha Pāka
kashaya avastha paka.body: Kashāya Avastha Pāka is the Sanskrit term for the astringent stage of digestion. It represents the principle of Vāta-predominant elimination and is associated with the nourishment of immature, asthāyi, Shukra or Ārtava Dhātu in the body. Located on the posterior part of the tongue, jihvā, and energetically linked to the colon, Kashāya stimulates emotions of fear, anxiety, and nervousness. Its Vipāka, the post-digestive effect, is Katu, which is catabolic and increases Vāta Dosha.

pakvashaya.title: Pakvashaya
pakvashaya.body: Pākvāshaya is the Sanskrit term for colon/ large intestine.

large intestine.title: Large intestine
large intestine.body: Where water is absorbed and waste is formed; the colon.

kashaya.title: Kashāya
kashaya.body: Kashāya is the Sanskrit term for the astringent taste, the sixth of the six essential rasas. It represents the principle of contraction and binding and is associated with the air and earth elements in the body.

apana vayu.title: Apāna Vāyu
apana vayu.body: Āpana Vāyu is the subdosha of Vāta related to the earth element. It is primarily located in the colon and pelvic cavity, represents the principle of eliminating flatulence, feces, and menses, as well as the movement of the fetus, and moves downward and outward.

ileocecal valve.title: Ileocecal valve
ileocecal valve.body: The ileocecal valve is a one-way muscular structure in the lower right abdomen that connects the ileum to the cecum. It prevents backflow of fecal matter and bacteria, regulates the flow of contents into the colon for nutrient absorption, and protects the small intestine from bacterial overgrowth.

cecum.title: Cecum
cecum.body: The cecum is the first pouch-like part of the large intestine, located in the lower right abdomen. It connects the small intestine (ileum) to the ascending colon, and the appendix is attached to its bottom. Its main functions include reabsorbing water and electrolytes from liquid waste (chyme) received from the small intestine, mixing digested waste with mucus to help it move smoothly into the colon, and housing beneficial gut bacteria that assist in the digestive process.

ascending colon.title: Ascending colon
ascending colon.body: The ascending colon is the part of the large intestine that connects the cecum to the transverse colon, located on the right side of the abdomen. Its main role is to absorb water and electrolytes from undigested food, turning liquid waste into solid stool.

hepatic flexure.title: Hepatic flexure
hepatic flexure.body: The hepatic flexure is a sharp 90-degree bend in the large intestine where the ascending colon turns into the horizontal transverse colon. Located in the upper right abdomen beneath the liver, its main role is to direct the flow of digestive waste. As stool moves up the right side, the hepatic flexure slows its progress, allowing the colon to absorb remaining water and electrolytes before the waste continues across the body.

transverse colon.title: Transverse colon
transverse colon.body: The transverse colon is the longest and most mobile section of the large intestine, extending horizontally across the upper abdomen from the right to the left side. Its primary functions include absorbing remaining water and salts from digested food and processing waste before storage and elimination. Additionally, it contains a healthy microbiome that synthesizes essential vitamins, such as Vitamin K and B vitamins, and breaks down bilirubin, contributing to the characteristic brown color of stool.

splenic flexure.title: Splenic flexure
splenic flexure.body: The splenic flexure is the sharp, upper-left bend in the large intestine where the transverse colon meets the descending colon, located just beneath the spleen. Its primary function is to redirect the flow of digested food and waste downward through the digestive tract. Due to its acute angle, the splenic flexure is a common site for gas to become trapped, which can lead to abdominal discomfort, bloating, or cramping.

descending colon.title: Descending colon
descending colon.body: The descending colon is the part of the large intestine that runs down the left side of the abdomen, connecting the transverse colon to the sigmoid colon. Its main functions are to absorb remaining water and electrolytes from indigestible food, solidify waste, and store feces before they are emptied into the rectum for elimination.

purisha.title: Purīsha
purisha.body: Purīsha is the Sanskrit term for feces or stool, one of the primary bodily wastes, malas. It represents the principle of elimination and support, helping to absorb minerals and water while providing essential structural stability to the colon wall, and is associated with the earth element in the body.

sigmoid colon.title: Sigmoid colon
sigmoid colon.body: The sigmoid colon is an S-shaped segment of the large intestine, measuring 10 to 15 inches, that connects the descending colon to the rectum. Its primary functions include storing solid waste, absorbing any remaining water and nutrients, and utilizing strong muscle contractions to propel feces into the rectum. The muscular walls of the sigmoid colon serve as a temporary holding area, preventing continuous pressure on the rectum. Its flexible structure also allows for the isolation and release of built-up gas without simultaneously expelling feces.

poshaka vata.title: Poshaka Vāta
poshaka vata.body: Poshaka Vāta is the Sanskrit term for the nourishing or precursor Vāta, the unstable or unprocessed form of the movement principle. It represents the principle of Vāta nourishment, is formed in the lower gut during the discrimination between essential nutrients and waste products, sāra kitta vivechana, and is associated with the ākāsha, ether, and vayu, air, elements in the body.

rectum.title: Rectum
rectum.body: The rectum is the final approximately 6 inches of the large intestine, connecting the colon to the anal canal. The rectum acts as a reservoir for fecal matter, allowing for voluntary control over bowel movements. As it fills, stretch receptors in its walls send signals to the brain, producing the urge to defecate. Additionally, while the colon primarily handles absorption, the rectum continues to absorb a minor amount of water and electrolytes.

anal canal.title: Anal canal
anal canal.body: The anal canal is the last 1 - 1.5 inches of the digestive tract, serving as the exit for feces from the rectum to the outside. It stays tightly closed to hold in feces, gas, and liquids. When it's time to eliminate waste, it relaxes and opens. It also senses the type of material coming (gas, solid, or liquid) to trigger the right response.

anus.title: Anus
anus.body: The anus is the opening at the end of the digestive tract where solid waste (feces) leaves the body.

ruksha.title: Ruksha Guna
ruksha.body: Rūksha is the Sanskrit term for the dry quality, representing the principle of dehydration and is associated with absorption and constipation in the body.

laghu.title: Laghu Guna
laghu.body: Laghu is the Sanskrit term for the light quality, representing the principle of alertness and is associated with catabolic reduction in the body.

khara.title: Khara Guna
khara.body: Khāra is the Sanskrit term for the rough quality, representing the principle of rigidity, and is associated with the cracking of the skin and bones in the body.

sukshma.title: Sukshma Guna
sukshma.body: Sūkshma is the Sanskrit term for the subtle quality, representing the principle of penetration and associated with entry into the body's minute capillaries.

chala.title: Chala Guna
chala.body: Chala is the Sanskrit term for the mobile quality, representing the principle of motion and is associated with shakiness and restlessness in the body.

vishada.title: Vishada Guna
vishada.body: Vishada is the Sanskrit term for the clear quality, representing the principle of purity and is associated with isolation and mental lucidity in the body.

akruti.title: Ākruti
akruti.body: Ākruti is a Sanskrit term that broadly translates to form, figure, shape, or appearance. In the context of Āyurveda, it has two primary clinical applications: assessing a person's physical appearance and examining a specific characteristic of the pulse. Volume corresponds to systolic blood pressure, and tension corresponds to diastolic blood pressure.

vishama agni.title: Vishama Āgni
vishama agni.body: Vishama Āgni is the Sanskrit term for irregular metabolism, one of the four clinical varieties of Āgni. It represents the principle of fluctuation and is associated with aggravated Vāta Dosha in the body.

sarpa.title: Sarpa Gati
sarpa.body: Sarpa Gati is the Sanskrit term for the cobra pulse, one of the primary animal gatis. It is primarily felt under the index finger, represents the principle of serpentine or slithering movement, is characterized as being thin, fast, and feeble, and is associated with Vāta Dosha and the ether and air elements.

tikshna.title: Tikshna Guna
tikshna.body: Tīkshna is the Sanskrit term for the sharp or penetrating quality, representing the principle of quick understanding and is associated with hyper-metabolism in the body.

drava.title: Drava Guna
drava.body: Drava is the Sanskrit term for the liquid quality, representing the principle of liquefaction and is associated with salivation and cohesiveness in the body.

snigdha.title: Snigdha Guna
snigdha.body: Snigdha is the Sanskrit term for the oily or unctuous quality, representing the principle of lubrication and is associated with moisture and compassion in the body.

saram.title: Sara Guna
saram.body: Sara is the Sanskrit term for the spreading or creeping quality, representing the principle of flowing movement and is associated with increased Pitta Dosha in the body.

visra.title: Visra
visra.body: Fleshy or fetid smell — a Pitta body-odor quality.

tikshna agni.title: Tikshna Āgni
tikshna agni.body: Tīkshna Āgni is the Sanskrit term for sharp metabolism or hypermetabolism, one of the four clinical varieties of Āgni. It represents the principle of intensity and is associated with aggravated Pitta Dosha in the body.

manduka.title: Manduka Gati
manduka.body: Mandūka Gati is the Sanskrit term for the frog pulse, one of the primary animal gatis. It is primarily felt under the middle finger, represents the principle of jumping or pounding movement, is characterized as being full, bounding, and hot, and is associated with Pitta Dosha and the fire and water elements.

guru.title: Guru Guna
guru.body: Guru is the Sanskrit term for the heavy quality, representing the principle of bulk nutrition and is associated with anabolic growth in the body.

manda.title: Manda Guna
manda.body: Manda is the Sanskrit term for the slow or dull quality, representing the principle of sluggishness and is associated with metabolic relaxation in the body.

shlakshna.title: Shlakshna Guna
shlakshna.body: Shlakshna is the Sanskrit term for the slimy or smooth quality, representing the principle of flexibility and is associated with joint lubrication in the body.

sandra.title: Sandra Guna
sandra.body: Sandra is the Sanskrit term for the dense quality, representing the principle of solidity and is associated with compactness and groundedness in the body.

mrudu.title: Mrudu Guna
mrudu.body: Mrudu is the Sanskrit term for the soft quality, representing the principle of tenderness and is associated with tissue relaxation in the body.

sthira.title: Sthira Guna
sthira.body: Sthira is the Sanskrit term for the static or stable quality, representing the principle of support and is associated with obstruction and fixity in the body.

picchila.title: Picchila Guna
picchila.body: Picchila is the Sanskrit term for the sticky quality, representing the principle of adhesiveness and is associated with a lack of clarity in the body.

avila.title: Avila Guna
avila.body: Āvila is the Sanskrit term for the cloudy quality, representing the principle of adhesiveness, and is associated with a lack of clarity in the body.

sthula.title: Sthula Guna
sthula.body: Sthūla is the Sanskrit term for the gross quality, representing the principle of bulk and is associated with obstruction and obesity in the body.

manda agni.title: Manda Āgni
manda agni.body: Manda Āgni is the Sanskrit term for slow or dull metabolism, one of the four clinical varieties of Āgni. It represents the principle of sluggishness and is associated with increased Kapha Dosha in the body.

hamsa.title: Hamsa Gati
hamsa.body: Hamsa Gati is the Sanskrit term for the swan pulse, one of the primary animal gatis. It is primarily felt under the ring finger, represents the principle of stable, wavy movement, is characterized as being deep, slow, and cool, and is associated with Kapha Dosha and the water and earth elements.

gunas.title: Guna
gunas.body: Guna is the Sanskrit term for an attribute or quality, representing the static nature of a substance and is associated with the potential energy stored within all organic and inorganic matter, as well as within thoughts and actions.

amla avastha paka.title: Amla Avastha Pāka
amla avastha paka.body: Amla Avastha Pāka is the Sanskrit term for the sour stage of digestion. It represents the principle of Pitta-predominant acidification and is associated with the nourishment of immature, asthāyi, Rakta Dhātu in the body. Located on the anterior outer sides of the tongue, jihvā, and energetically linked to the lungs, Amla stimulates emotions like jealousy and hate. Its Vipāka, the post-digestive effect, is Amla, which is metabolic and increases Pitta Dosha.

enzymes.title: Enzymes
enzymes.body: Enzymes are specialized proteins that act as biological catalysts to speed up biochemical reactions, specifically the breakdown and synthesis of various molecules within the body. Their primary function is to facilitate and accelerate these reactions, which is most prominent in chemical digestion. During this process, enzymes and acids decompose food substances into smaller, usable molecules that can be absorbed as basic nutrients. These catalysts are active throughout the body, from lysosomes that use them to digest worn-out cell structures to the small intestine, where they process proteins, fats, and carbohydrates.

kathina.title: Kathina Guna
kathina.body: Kathina is the Sanskrit term for the hard quality, representing the principle of strength and is associated with callousness and rigidity in the body.

pancha mahabhutas.title: Pañcha Mahābhūtas
pancha mahabhutas.body: Pañcha Mahābhūtas is the Sanskrit term for the five basic elements, which serve as the fundamental building blocks for all matter in the universe. They represent the principles of freedom ākāsha, ether, movement vāyu, air, transformation āgni, fire, cohesiveness āpas, water, and stability pruthivī, earth, and combine in specific proportions to form the three biological organizations, tridosha.

rakta.title: Rakta
rakta.body: Rakta (blood tissue) — the second bodily tissue (dhātu); carries oxygen and vitality, and governs circulation and complexion.

mamsa.title: Māmsa
mamsa.body: Māmsa (muscle tissue) — the third dhātu; provides strength, movement, and physical form.

meda.title: Meda
meda.body: Meda (fat / adipose tissue) — the fourth dhātu; lubricates, insulates, and stores energy.

asthi.title: Asthi
asthi.body: Asthi (bone tissue) — the fifth dhātu; gives the body structure, support, and protection.

majja.title: Majjā
majja.body: Majjā (bone marrow and nerve tissue) — the sixth dhātu; fills the bones and carries nerve impulses.

shukra artava.title: Shukra / Ārtava
shukra artava.body: Shukra / Ārtava (reproductive tissue) — the seventh and most refined dhātu; governs reproduction and, at its essence, vitality (ojas).

rajah.title: Rajah
rajah.body: Rajah — menstrual flow; the monthly discharge associated with the reproductive tissue.

stanya.title: Stanya
stanya.body: Stanya — breast milk; a secondary tissue (upadhātu) nourished from rasa (plasma).

mutra.title: Mūtra
mutra.body: Mūtra — urine; one of the three primary wastes (malas), the body’s liquid waste.

sveda.title: Sveda
sveda.body: Sveda — sweat; the waste (mala) of the fat tissue (meda); regulates temperature and skin moisture.

mano.title: Mano
mano.body: Mano — the mind; the seat of thought, emotion, and perception, linking the senses to consciousness.

abhyantara marga.title: Abhyantara Mārga
abhyantara marga.body: Abhyantara Mārga is the Sanskrit term for the internal pathway, representing the innermost channel of the body. It consists of the gastrointestinal tract, Mahā Srotas, is associated with the Endoderm embryological layer, and is the primary site for the accumulation and provocation (Sañchaya and Prakopa) stages of disease.

ambu vaha srotas.title: Ambu Vaha Srotas
ambu vaha srotas.body:
Ambu Vaha Srotas, also known as Udaka Vaha Srotas, is the Sanskrit term for the water-regulating channel, one of the receiving channels. It represents the principle of hydration, electrolyte balance, and body temperature regulation, functioning to moisten tissues and select liquid wastes.

Mūla: the soft palate, tālu, pancreas, kloma, and the third ventricle of the brain

Mārga: the mucous membrane of the gastrointestinal tract, Maha Srotas

Mukha: the kidneys, vrukka, tongue, jihva, and pores of the skin

Mala: urine, mūtra, sweat, sveda

anna vaha srotas.title: Anna Vaha Srotas
anna vaha srotas.body:
Anna Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the food-carrying channel, one of the receiving channels. It represents the principle of digestion, absorption, and assimilation of nutrients, corresponding to the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the ileocecal valve.

Mūla: the esophagus and stomach fundus (greater curvature)

Mārga: the GI tract from the lips through to the ileocecal valve

Mukha: the ileocecal valve and mouth

Mala: feces, purīsha

artava dhatu.title: Ārtava Dhātu
artava dhatu.body:
Ārtava Dhātu is the Sanskrit term for the female reproductive tissue. It represents the principle of ovulation and conception, prajanana, functioning to continue human life through the union of male and female energy.

Upa-Dhātu: Ojas, the pure essence of all tissues

Mala: none, pubic and axillary hair are functionally related

artava vaha srotas.title: Ārtava Vaha Srotas
artava vaha srotas.body:
Ārtava Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the female reproductive channel, one of the nourishing channels. It represents the principle of ovulation, conception, and the production of ojas, including the ovaries and uterus.

Mūla: the ovaries and areola of the nipples

Mārga: the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervical canal, and vaginal passage

Mukha: the labia, yoni oshtha

Mala: none, pubic and axillary hair are functionally related

asthi dhatu.title: Asthi Dhātu
asthi dhatu.body:
Asthi Dhātu is the Sanskrit term for the bone tissue, the densest tissue in the body. It represents the principle of structural support and protection, dhārana, forming the skeletal framework that protects vital organs and provides the internal shape for the head, face, and limbs.

Upa-Dhātu: teeth, danta, and cartilage, taruna asthi

Mala: hair, kesha, and nails, nakha

asthi vaha srotas.title: Asthi Vaha Srotas
asthi vaha srotas.body:
Asthi Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the bone tissue channel, one of the nourishing channels. It represents the principle of structural support and protection, dhārana, functioning to form the skeletal framework.

Mūla: the pelvic girdle and sacrum

Mārga: the skeletal system

Mukha: nails, nakha and hair, kesha

Mala: hair, kesha, and nails, nakha

avila guna.title: Avila Guna
avila guna.body: Avila is the Sanskrit term for the cloudy quality, representing the principle of adhesiveness, and is associated with a lack of clarity in the body.

bahya marga.title: Bāhya Mārga
bahya marga.body: Bāhya Mārga is the Sanskrit term for the external or superficial pathway, representing the principle of peripheral circulation. It consists of the channels that carry Rasa and Rakta Dhātus, plasma and blood, is associated with the Ectoderm embryological layer, and is the primary site for the spread, Prasara, stages of disease.

chala guna.title: Chala Guna
chala guna.body: Chala is the Sanskrit term for the mobile quality, representing the principle of motion and is associated with shakiness and restlessness in the body.

drava guna.title: Drava Guna
drava guna.body: Drava is the Sanskrit term for the liquid quality, representing the principle of liquefaction and is associated with salivation and cohesiveness in the body.

guna.title: Guna
guna.body: Guna is the Sanskrit term for an attribute or quality, representing the static nature of a substance and is associated with the potential energy stored within all organic and inorganic matter, as well as within thoughts and actions.

guru guna.title: Guru Guna
guru guna.body: Guru is the Sanskrit term for the heavy quality, representing the principle of bulk nutrition and is associated with anabolic growth in the body.

hamsa gati.title: Hamsa Gati
hamsa gati.body: Hamsa Gati is the Sanskrit term for the swan pulse, one of the primary animal gatis. It is primarily felt under the ring finger, represents the principle of stable, wavy movement, is characterized as being deep, slow, and cool, and is associated with Kapha Dosha and the water and earth elements.

kathina guna.title: Kathina Guna
kathina guna.body: Kathina is the Sanskrit term for the hard quality, representing the principle of strength and is associated with callousness and rigidity in the body.

khara guna.title: Khara Guna
khara guna.body: Khara is the Sanskrit term for the rough quality, representing the principle of rigidity, and is associated with the cracking of the skin and bones in the body.

laghu guna.title: Laghu Guna
laghu guna.body: Laghu is the Sanskrit term for the light quality, representing the principle of alertness and is associated with catabolic reduction in the body.

madhyama marga.title: Madhyama Mārga
madhyama marga.body: Madhyama Mārga is the Sanskrit term for the middle or deep pathway, representing the principle of vital organ and deep tissue involvement. It includes the deep connective tissues, the subsequent five biological tissues (Māmsa, Meda, Asthi, Majjā, and Shukra/Ārtava), and the vital organs such as the brain, heart, and kidneys, and is associated with the Mesoderm embryological layer, and is the primary site for the deposition, manifestation, and disease differentiation, Sthāna Samshraya, Vyakti, and Bheda, stages of disease.

majja dhatu.title: Majjā Dhātu
majja dhatu.body:
Majjā Dhātu is the Sanskrit term for the nerve tissue and bone marrow, the sixth biological tissue. It represents the principle of filling bone spaces, pūrana, functioning to maintain communication, memory, coordination, and the flow of intelligence through the central and peripheral nervous systems.

Upa-Dhātu: lacrimal secretions, ashru

Mala: oily secretions in the eyes, akshi vitta sneha, and mucosal discharges

majja vaha srotas.title: Majjā Vaha Srotas
majja vaha srotas.body:
Majjā Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the nerve and bone marrow channel, one of the nourishing channels. It represents the principle of communication, memory, and filling spaces (pūrana), functioning to maintain coordination and higher mental functions.

Mūla (root): the brain, spinal cord, bone marrow, and joints (sandhi)

Mārga (passage): the central, sympathetic, and parasympathetic nervous systems

Mukha (opening): the synaptic space and neuromuscular cleft

Mala: oily secretions in the eyes, akshi vitta sneha, and mucosal discharges

mamsa dhatu.title: Māmsa Dhātu
mamsa dhatu.body:
Māmsa Dhātu is the Sanskrit term for the muscle tissue, the third biological tissue. It represents the principle of plastering, lepana, providing support, strength, coordination, and locomotion while covering and protecting the delicate internal organs.

Upa-Dhātu: muscle fat, vasā, and the six layers of skin, tvacha

Mala: khamala (nasal crust, earwax, sebaceous secretions, dental tartar, and smegma)

mamsa vaha srotas.title: Māmsa Vaha Srotas
mamsa vaha srotas.body:
Māmsa Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the muscle tissue channel, one of the nourishing channels. It represents the principle of strength, form, and coordination, functioning to provide support and cover the delicate organs.

Mūla: the fascia, six layers of skin, tvacha, small tendons, snāyu, and mesoderm

Mārga: the entire muscle system

Mukha: the pores of the skin and sites of khamala

Mala: khamala (nasal crust, earwax, sebaceous secretions, dental tartar, and smegma)

manda guna.title: Manda Guna
manda guna.body: Manda is the Sanskrit term for the slow or dull quality, representing the principle of sluggishness and is associated with metabolic relaxation in the body.

manduka gati.title: Manduka Gati
manduka gati.body: Mandūka Gati is the Sanskrit term for the frog pulse, one of the primary animal gatis. It is primarily felt under the middle finger, represents the principle of jumping or pounding movement, is characterized as being full, bounding, and hot, and is associated with Pitta Dosha and the fire and water elements.

mano vaha srotas.title: Mano Vaha Srotas
mano vaha srotas.body:
Mano Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the mind-carrying channel, the pathway of the entire person. It represents the principle of thinking, feeling, inquiring, and memory, serving as the bridge through which perception becomes attention and understanding throughout the whole body.

Mūla: the heart, cardiac plexus, brain, and chakra system

Mārga: the entire body

Mukha: the marma points and the five sensory organs (ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose)

Mala: excess rajas and tamas qualities

meda dhatu.title: Meda Dhātu
meda dhatu.body:
Meda Dhātu is the Sanskrit term for the adipose or fat tissue, the fourth biological tissue. It represents the principle of lubrication, snehan, functioning to store energy as a food reservoir, provide insulation, and manifest personal love and softness in the body.

Upa-Dhātu: tendons, sinews, ligaments, and flat muscles, snāyu

Mala: sweat, sveda

meda vaha srotas.title: Meda Vaha Srotas
meda vaha srotas.body:
Meda Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the fat-carrying channel, one of the nourishing channels. It represents the principle of lubrication, insulation, and personal love, functioning to store energy and add bulk to the body.

Mūla: the omentum and adrenal glands, vrukka

Mārga: the subcutaneous fat tissue, meda

Mukha: the sweat glands

Mala: sweat, sveda

mrudu guna.title: Mrudu Guna
mrudu guna.body: Mrudu is the Sanskrit term for the soft quality, representing the principle of tenderness and is associated with tissue relaxation in the body.

mutra vaha srotas.title: Mūtra Vaha Srotas
mutra vaha srotas.body:
Mūtra Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the urinary channel, one of the channels of elimination. It represents the principle of electrolyte balance and elimination of liquid waste, functioning to maintain blood pressure and excrete nitrogenous toxins.

Mūla: the kidneys

Mārga: the ureters, bladder, and urethra

Mukha: the urethral opening

Mala: none

ojas.title: Ojas
ojas.body: Ojas is the Sanskrit term for the vital essence, the pure essence of Kapha Dosha and the water element in particular. It represents the principle of natural immunity and vitality, serving as a superfine biological substance that circulates via the heart throughout the body to maintain the resistance and stability of all tissues. It is composed of two types: Apara Ojas, unprocessed, which circulates throughout the system, and Para Ojas, superior, which consists of eight drops that remain in the heart to maintain the life of the individual.

picchila guna.title: Picchila Guna
picchila guna.body: Picchila is the Sanskrit term for the sticky quality, representing the principle of adhesiveness and is associated with a lack of clarity in the body.

prana.title: Prāna
prana.body: Prāna is the Sanskrit term for the vital life force, the pure essence of Vāta Dosha and the ākāsha, ether element in particular. It represents the principle of cellular communication and respiration, serving as the flow of intelligence that governs all motor and sensory functions, oxygenation, and the pulsation of the heart. In its role as the bridge between body, mind, and consciousness, it directs attention to create perception and enkindles the central bodily fire, Āgni, to express the body's natural intelligence.

prana vaha srotas.title: Prāna Vaha Srotas
prana vaha srotas.body:
Prāna Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the respiratory channel, one of the receiving channels. It represents the principle of respiration, maintaining life functions, and communication with the higher self, functioning to maintain the flow of intelligence between the body and mind.

Mūla: the left chamber of the heart and the entire gastrointestinal tract, Maha Srotas

Mārga: the respiratory tract, including the bronchial tree, alveoli, larynx, and pharynx

Mukha: nose, nasa

Mala: carbon dioxide

purisha vaha srotas.title: Purisha Vaha Srotas
purisha vaha srotas.body:
Purīsha Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the feces carrying channel, one of the channels of elimination. It represents the principle of absorption of minerals and elimination of solid waste, functioning to provide structural stability to the colon.

Mūla: the cecum, rectum, guda, and sigmoid colon

Mārga: the large intestine

Mukha: the anal orifice

Mala: none

rajah vaha srotas.title: Rajah Vaha Srotas
rajah vaha srotas.body:
Rajah Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the menstrual channel, one of the specific female nourishing channels. It represents the principle of menstrual cleansing, functioning to clear away the unfertilized ovum and the old endometrial lining after each cycle.

Mūla, Mārga, and Mukha: these components share structural confluence with Ārtava Vaha Srotas

rakta dhatu.title: Rakta Dhātu
rakta dhatu.body:
Rakta Dhātu is the Sanskrit term for the blood tissue, specifically the red blood cells. It represents the principle of life function, jīvana, responsible for oxygenation, enthusiasm, and maintaining the life of every cell while serving as a bridge between the internal and external environments.

Upa-Dhātu: blood vessels, sirā, and small tendons or sinews, kandara

Mala: Poshaka Pitta, precursor Pitta, which manifests as bile

rakta vaha srotas.title: Rakta Vaha Srotas
rakta vaha srotas.body:
Rakta Raha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the blood-carrying channel, one of the nourishing channels. It represents the principle of oxygenation, life function, and enthusiasm, responsible for transporting nutrients, hormones, and heat.

Mūla: the liver, yakrut, and spleen, plīha

Mārga: the arteries and circulatory system

Mukha: the arteriole-venous junctions

Mala: Poshaka Pitta, precursor Pitta, which manifests as bile

rasa vaha srotas.title: Rasa Vaha Srotas
rasa vaha srotas.body:
Rasa Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the plasma channel, one of the nourishing channels. It represents the principle of nutrition, immunity, and faith, functioning to provide nourishment to every cell in the body.

Mūla: the right chamber of the heart and the ten great vessels

Mārga: the venous and lymphatic systems

Mukha: the arteriole-venous junctions

Mala: Poshaka Kapha, precursor Kapha, which manifests as mucus, kleda

ruksha guna.title: Ruksha Guna
ruksha guna.body: Ruksha is the Sanskrit term for the dry quality, representing the principle of dehydration and is associated with absorption and constipation in the body.

sandra guna.title: Sandra Guna
sandra guna.body: Sandra is the Sanskrit term for the dense quality, representing the principle of solidity and is associated with compactness and groundedness in the body.

sara guna.title: Sara Guna
sara guna.body: Sara is the Sanskrit term for the spreading or creeping quality, representing the principle of flowing movement and is associated with increased Pitta Dosha in the body.

sarpa gati.title: Sarpa Gati
sarpa gati.body: Sarpa Gati is the Sanskrit term for the cobra pulse, one of the primary animal gatis. It is primarily felt under the index finger, represents the principle of serpentine or slithering movement, is characterized as being thin, fast, and feeble, and is associated with Vāta Dosha and the ether and air elements.

shita guna.title: Shīta Guna
shita guna.body: Shīta is the Sanskrit term for the cold quality, representing the principle of contraction and is associated with reduced metabolic rate in the body.

shlakshna guna.title: Shlakshna Guna
shlakshna guna.body: Shlakshna is the Sanskrit term for the slimy or smooth quality, representing the principle of flexibility and is associated with joint lubrication in the body.

shukra dhatu.title: Shukra Dhātu
shukra dhatu.body:
Shukra Dhātu is the Sanskrit term for the male reproductive tissue. It represents the principle of procreation, prajanana, supreme intelligence, and emotional release, serving as the refined essence of all tissues that ultimately produces ojas for vigor and vitality.

Upa-Dhātu: Ojas, the pure essence of all tissues

Mala: none, pubic and axillary hair are functionally related

shukra vaha srotas.title: Shukra Vaha Srotas
shukra vaha srotas.body:
Shukra Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the male reproductive channel, one of the nourishing channels. It represents the principle of procreation (prajanana), supreme intelligence, and emotional release, functioning to produce semen and ojas.

Mūla: the testicles and nipples

Mārga: the vas deferens, epididymis, prostate, urethra, and urinogenital tract

Mukha: the urethral opening

Mala: none, pubic and axillary hair are functionally related

snigdha guna.title: Snigdha Guna
snigdha guna.body: Snigdha is the Sanskrit term for the oily or unctuous quality, representing the principle of lubrication and is associated with moisture and compassion in the body.

stanya vaha srotas.title: Stanya Vaha Srotas
stanya vaha srotas.body:
Stanya Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the lactation channel, one of the specific female nourishing channels. It represents the principle of lactation, functioning to create and transport mother's milk.

Mūla: the lactiferous glands and Rasa Dhātu

Mārga: the lactiferous ducts

Mukha: the nipple ducts

Mala: none

sthira guna.title: Sthira Guna
sthira guna.body: Sthira is the Sanskrit term for the static or stable quality, representing the principle of support and is associated with obstruction and fixity in the body.

sthula guna.title: Sthula Guna
sthula guna.body: Sthula is the Sanskrit term for the gross quality, representing the principle of bulk and is associated with obstruction and obesity in the body.

sukshma guna.title: Sukshma Guna
sukshma guna.body: Sukshma is the Sanskrit term for the subtle quality, representing the principle of penetration and associated with entry into the body's minute capillaries.

sveda vaha srotas.title: Sveda Vaha Srotas
sveda vaha srotas.body:
Sveda Vaha Srotas is the Sanskrit term for the sweat-carrying channel, one of the channels of elimination. It represents the principle of body temperature regulation and skin lubrication, functioning to excrete excess liquid wastes.

Mūla: the sweat glands and sebaceous glands

Mārga: the sweat ducts and sebaceous ducts

Mukha: the pores of the skin and openings of the sweat glands

Mala: none

tejas.title: Tejas
tejas.body: Tejas is the Sanskrit term for radiant energy or pure intelligence, the pure essence of Pitta Dosha and the fire element in particular. It represents the principle of digestion, transformation, and cellular intelligence, governing the "cooking" of everything taken into the body, from food and liquids to thoughts and emotions. Tejas is responsible for maintaining the semi-permeability of cell membranes and manifests as the luminosity of the aura, intelligence, and the flame of attention.

tikshna guna.title: Tikshna Guna
tikshna guna.body: Tīkshna is the Sanskrit term for the sharp or penetrating quality, representing the principle of quick understanding and is associated with hyper-metabolism in the body.

ushna guna.title: Ushna Guna
ushna guna.body: Ushna is the Sanskrit term for the hot quality, representing the principle of digestion and is associated with increased circulation in the body.

vishada guna.title: Vishada Guna
vishada guna.body: Vishada is the Sanskrit term for the clear quality, representing the principle of purity and is associated with isolation and mental lucidity in the body.

lower esophageal sphincter.title: Lower Esophageal Sphincter
lower esophageal sphincter.body: The Lower Esophageal Sphincter (LES) is at the bottom of the esophagus, connecting it to the stomach. It relaxes to let food enter the stomach and closes tightly to prevent stomach acid and digestive juices from flowing back into the esophagus.

nasal cavity.title: Nasal Cavity
nasal cavity.body: The nasal cavity is the air-filled space behind the nose, primarily responsible for conditioning inhaled air by warming, humidifying, and filtering it before it reaches the lungs. It traps dust and pathogens with mucus and cilia, supports the sense of smell, and aids in voice resonance. The nasal cavity consists of three main parts: the vestibule, which has coarse hairs to filter large particles; the respiratory region, lined with mucous membranes and cilia to clear dirt and germs; and the olfactory region at the top, containing sensory receptors for the sense of smell.

parotid gland.title: Parotid Gland
parotid gland.body: The parotid gland is the largest of the three main salivary glands, located just below and in front of each ear. Its primary function is to secrete a thin, watery saliva rich in the enzyme amylase, which initiates the digestion of starches. This saliva lubricates the mouth, making it easier to chew and swallow food, while also helping to wash away bacteria and protect tooth enamel from cavities.

sublingual gland.title: Sublingual Gland
sublingual gland.body: The sublingual gland is the smallest of the major salivary glands, located under the mucous membrane in the floor of the mouth, on either side of the tongue. Its primary function is to secrete thick, mucus-rich saliva, which lubricates food for easier swallowing, keeps the mouth moist, and aids in early digestion. The mucus coats food to form a slippery bolus for swallowing and protects the oral mucosa from dryness and irritation.

submandibular gland.title: Submandibular Gland
submandibular gland.body: The submandibular gland consists of a pair of major salivary glands located beneath the lower jaw. Its primary function is to produce up to 70% of resting saliva, which lubricates the mouth, facilitates swallowing, chemically breaks down starches through enzymes, and protects against oral bacteria and decay.

upper esophageal sphincter.title: Upper Esophageal Sphincter
upper esophageal sphincter.body: The Upper Esophageal Sphincter (UES) is located at the top of the esophagus. It opens during swallowing to allow food and liquids in and closes to prevent air and contents from entering the trachea.

digestive system.title: Digestive system
digestive system.body: The organs that work together to break food down into nutrients the body can absorb, and to remove what is left over.

mouth.title: Mouth
mouth.body: The oral cavity, or mouth, is the first part of the digestive tract, extending from the lips to the back of the throat, connecting to the pharynx. It contains essential structures like the teeth, tongue, palate, and openings for salivary glands. Its key functions include mechanically breaking down food through chewing and starting chemical digestion with saliva, shaping airflow and producing sounds for speech, evaluating food through sensory receptors called taste buds, and serving as a secondary airway when nasal breathing is restricted.

large intestinecolon.title: Large intestine/colon
large intestinecolon.body: Where water is absorbed and waste is formed; the colon.

ingestion.title: Ingestion
ingestion.body: Taking food into the body through the mouth — the first stage of digestion.

propulsion.title: Propulsion
propulsion.body: The movement of food along the digestive tract, largely by peristalsis.

digestion.title: Digestion
digestion.body: The breakdown of food into small molecules the body can absorb.

absorption.title: Absorption
absorption.body: The passage of nutrients from the gut into the blood and lymph.

elimination.title: Elimination
elimination.body: The removal of undigested waste from the body as feces.

sara.title: Sara
sara.body: Sara is the Sanskrit term for the spreading or creeping quality, representing the principle of flowing movement and is associated with increased Pitta Dosha in the body.

pitta.title: Pitta
pitta.body: Pitta Dosha is the Sanskrit term for the fire or transformation principle, the second of the three biological organizations (tridosha). It represents the principle of transformation, governing digestion, metabolism, and body temperature, and is associated with the fire and water elements.

hima.title: Hima
hima.body: Cool — a Kapha quality, giving cool clammy skin and slow digestion.

para ojas.title: Para Ojas
para ojas.body: Para Ojas is the Sanskrit term for superior or superfine Ojas, representing the pure and fully processed essence of all seven Dhātus. It consists of exactly eight drops, each roughly the size of a poppy seed, which stay permanently in the heart to maintain the individual’s life and serve as the stable foundation for the body's vital essence.

cholecystokinin cck.title: Cholecystokinin CCK
cholecystokinin cck.body: Cholecystokinin (CCK) is a local hormone produced and secreted by the small intestine, specifically the duodenum, that plays a vital role in coordinating chemical digestion. Its primary functions include stimulating the pancreas to release digestive enzymes and signaling the gallbladder and liver to discharge bile into the gastrointestinal tract. Furthermore, CCK serves as a key integrator between body systems; because receptors for the hormone are also located in the brain and spleen, it effectively links digestive activity to both the nervous and immune systems.

sublingual glands.title: Sublingual glands
sublingual glands.body: The sublingual gland is the smallest of the major salivary glands, located under the mucous membrane in the floor of the mouth, on either side of the tongue. Its primary function is to secrete thick, mucus-rich saliva, which lubricates food for easier swallowing, keeps the mouth moist, and aids in early digestion. The mucus coats food to form a slippery bolus for swallowing and protects the oral mucosa from dryness and irritation.

kapha.title: Kapha
kapha.body: Kapha Dosha is the Sanskrit term for the water or structure principle, the third of the three biological organizations (tridosha). It represents the principle of substance, providing the body's structure, lubrication, and cohesiveness, and is associated with the water and earth elements.

enzyme.title: Enzyme
enzyme.body: Enzymes are specialized proteins that act as biological catalysts to speed up biochemical reactions, specifically the breakdown and synthesis of various molecules within the body. Their primary function is to facilitate and accelerate these reactions, which is most prominent in chemical digestion. During this process, enzymes and acids decompose food substances into smaller, usable molecules that can be absorbed as basic nutrients. These catalysts are active throughout the body, from lysosomes that use them to digest worn-out cell structures to the small intestine, where they process proteins, fats, and carbohydrates.

brains grey matter.title: Brain's grey matter
brains grey matter.body: Grey matter consists of the areas in the brain and spinal cord made primarily of unmyelinated axons, cell bodies, dendrites, and glial cells. In the brain, it is found in the cerebral cortex, which is the thin outer rim of the cerebrum, and in deep internal structures known as basal ganglia. Functionally, grey matter acts as the integration center for complex cognitive processes, including conscious thinking, problem-solving, memory, learning, and sensory perception. It is also the site where Sādhaka Pitta processes comprehension and emotions, effectively coordinating motor planning and the body's higher mental functions.

acids.title: Acids
acids.body: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is a highly acidic electrolyte compound secreted by the stomach as a primary component of gastric juice. Its primary digestive functions include initiating the chemical breakdown of proteins and activating the enzyme pepsin from its inactive form, pepsinogen. Beyond digestion, it serves as a critical nonspecific immune defense by killing or destroying bacteria and other pathogens that enter the body with food. Because of its potency, the stomach produces a protective layer of mucus to prevent the acid from damaging the stomach wall or causing ulcers.

mall intestine.title: Mall intestine
mall intestine.body: Where most digestion and absorption of nutrients occurs.

appendix.title: Appendix
appendix.body: The appendix is a small, tube-shaped pouch attached to the cecum, large intestine. Its main functions are storing helpful gut bacteria and supporting the immune system.

pruthivi.title: Pruthivī
pruthivi.body: Pruthivī is the Sanskrit term for the Earth element, the fifth of the five basic elements, pañcha mahābhūtas. It represents the principle of stability and is associated with mechanical energy in the body.

agnis.title: Āgnis
agnis.body: Āgni is the Sanskrit term for the Fire element, the third of the five basic elements, pañcha mahābhūtas. It represents the principle of transformation and is associated with radiant energy in the body.

mamsa medha asthi majja shukra artava.title: Māmsa, Medha, Asthi, Majjā, Shukra, Ārtava
